records.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A01 Broken Access Control
records.study_design: eight of ten categories ranked from contributed application-testing data, two promoted by a community survey, with CVE exploitability and impact scores folded into the ordering
records.population: over 2.8 million applications tested; 589 CWEs considered and 248 mapped across the ten categories; about 175,000 CVE records mapped to CWEs. A01 alone maps 40 CWEs, 1,839,701 occurrences and 32,654 CVEs, average incidence 3.74 percent and maximum 20.15 percent
records.licence: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported, as stated on the 2025 introduction page. Other OWASP surfaces state CC BY-SA 4.0, so the version differs by document and cannot be assumed
records.finding: Failure to decide correctly who may touch what is the single largest measured defect class in web software, and the named failure shapes are mundane: no deny-by-default, an identifier in a URL that nobody checks belongs to the caller, write verbs left unguarded when the read verb was guarded, and a token whose claims are trusted without being verified. The prevention list is equally plain: decide on the server, deny unless permitted, enforce record ownership rather than open create-read-update-delete in anything multi-tenant, reuse one mechanism rather than writing the check per handler, and test the refusals.
records.applicability_limits: Incidence is measured over applications a contributing tool or tester examined, so it reports what scanners and testers find rather than what attackers exploit or what a breach costs. Two of the ten categories are voted rather than measured. The numbers say nothing about which authorisation model to choose.
records.counter_evidence: The same data basis makes A01's position partly an artefact of detectability: access-control faults are cheap for a tester to find in bulk, which inflates occurrence counts relative to classes that need deep analysis. Occurrence count is not severity.

records.source: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Authorization Cheat Sheet
records.version_or_commit: live page, no version or revision date shown on the document itself
records.finding: Two rules do most of the work and neither depends on the model chosen: refuse unless something explicitly permits, and run the check at one trusted layer that every request passes through rather than per handler, because getting it right on most requests is the same as getting it wrong. The page then takes a side on the model question and prefers attribute-based and relationship-based authorisation over roles, on the grounds that roles multiply when a permission depends on anything other than who the person is, and that a tenant boundary is one of the things roles express badly.
records.applicability_limits: Practitioner consensus guidance with no measurement behind the preference; it names role explosion as the reason without quantifying where it starts to bite or what the migration costs.
records.counter_evidence: It disagrees with the standards position at FRAG-IDENTITY-ACCESS-03, where the value claimed for roles is administrative, not expressive: fewer things for a human to get wrong when provisioning and deprovisioning. Both can be right, because they are answering different questions.

records.source: NIST Role Based Access Control project, and ANSI/INCITS 359 as the RBAC standard
records.study_design: the page cites an economic analysis of RBAC adoption commissioned by NIST, final report December 2010
records.population: United States industry adoption, aggregated; the page reports the estimate rather than the method
records.version_or_commit: INCITS 359-2012, revising ANSI/INCITS 359-2004; project page last updated 2026-03-04
records.licence: NIST web content is a United States Government work and is not subject to domestic copyright. The INCITS 359 standard itself is an INCITS publication sold under its own copyright, so the model is public and the normative text is not
records.finding: Roles are a standardised, revised and still current model whose claimed benefit is administrative rather than expressive: the saving is in provisioning, deprovisioning and reduced employee downtime, which is where the cited estimate of about 1.1 billion dollars of industry saving comes from. The standard also carries the machinery for the two things that break naive role systems, role hierarchies and mutually exclusive roles, which is worth knowing before anyone concludes roles cannot express separation of duties.
records.applicability_limits: The economic estimate is an aggregate over large United States organisations with formal joiner-mover-leaver processes; it has no bearing on a venture with five people and no provisioning workflow at all. The normative text sits behind a paid standard, so what is freely readable is the model summary rather than the requirements.
records.counter_evidence: The saving is claimed for administration, which is exactly the dimension a small venture has least of, so the strongest published argument for roles is the one that transfers worst to the estate this pack serves.

records.source: NIST SP 800-162, Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations
records.version_or_commit: Update 2, final; first published January 2014, latest update 2 August 2019
records.licence: United States Government work, not subject to domestic copyright
records.finding: The attribute-based definition is deliberately wider than roles: a decision evaluates attributes of the subject, of the object, of the requested operation and sometimes of the environment against a written rule, so a permission can depend on the clearance, the record's classification, the time of day or the network the request came from without any of those becoming a role. The cost is that the decision is only as good as the attributes, which have to come from somewhere, be current, and be trusted.
records.applicability_limits: Written for United States federal agencies with existing attribute authorities and identity governance; it defines and considers rather than prescribing, and it gives no acceptance threshold. It has not been revised since 2019, so it predates the relationship-based systems now in production and says nothing about them.
records.counter_evidence: Its own currency is the counter-evidence: the canonical official definition of ABAC is seven years without revision while the field it describes has moved, which argues for reading it as vocabulary rather than as current practice.

records.source: Zanzibar: Google's Consistent, Global Authorization System
records.study_design: system and experience paper reporting production measurements from one deployment; no control arm and no comparison against an alternative design
records.population: more than 1,500 namespaces from hundreds of Google client services, over 2 trillion relation tuples occupying close to 100 terabytes, replicated in more than 30 locations, served by more than 10,000 servers; load figures sampled over 7 days in December 2018
records.version_or_commit: USENIX ATC 2019 proceedings, pages 33 to 46; production experience of more than 5 years at time of writing
records.licence: USENIX open-access proceedings. The paper carries no licence statement in its own text and the presentation page refused automated access at this reading, so reuse terms were not verified and only facts, not wording, are carried here
records.finding: Relationship-based authorisation reduces to one durable shape: a tuple saying that a user, or a set of users named by another object and relation, stands in a named relation to an object, plus rewrite rules that derive relations from other relations. That is enough to express nested groups, inheritance from a folder to its contents, and sharing to a person who has no role at all. The hard part is not expressing the permission, it is consistency: revoking access and then adding content can leak the new content to the removed user unless the check respects the causal order of the two changes, which the system solves by having the client store an opaque token per content version and pass it back on the check.
records.applicability_limits: The design is inseparable from a globally consistent database with synchronised clocks, a specialised set-computation index, request hedging and per-client quotas. Reported at Google's scale and operated by a dedicated team; nothing in the paper says the shape is right for a system with three tenants and one database, and nothing measures it against roles or attributes.
records.counter_evidence: The paper's own lessons section reports that hot spots, where many objects indirectly depend on one heavily shared group or one node high in a hierarchy, are a critical availability problem needing caching, prefetch and deduplication to contain, and that isolation safeguards had to be added to stop one misbehaving client damaging others. The consistency guarantee also costs the client work: the token has to be stored with the content and passed back, so a client that skips it silently loses the property the design exists for.
records.review: on-change-of:a published independent evaluation of relationship-based authorisation

records.version_or_commit: documentation page shown as updated 2026-08-13; repository at github.com/openfga/openfga, about 5.6k stars at this reading; accepted into the CNCF on 2022-09-14 and moved to incubating on 2025-10-28
records.finding: The Zanzibar shape is available as an ordinary open-source service, which changes the fork from build against buy into adopt against model it yourself. A type definition names the relations an object can carry, a relationship tuple asserts one of them, and a check answers whether a relation holds. Two additions matter for a small system: conditions on tuples, evaluated with a general expression language, which lets one engine carry the attribute-shaped part of a policy, and contextual tuples supplied per request and never stored, which cover facts known only at request time.
records.applicability_limits: Adopting it means running and backing up a second stateful service on the authorisation path and keeping its tuples in step with the application's own data. The concepts page states no limits on recursion depth, list operations or consistency modes, so those have to be read from the reference documentation before any capacity claim is made.
records.counter_evidence: Incubating rather than graduated in the CNCF, and the production track record the project points at is one vendor's own product. Conditions blur the clean separation the model is praised for: once a tuple carries an expression, the store holds policy as well as relationships, which is the coupling attribute systems are criticised for.

records.source: OASIS eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) Version 3.0
records.licence: Copyright OASIS Open 2013, all rights reserved, under the OASIS Intellectual Property Rights Policy, which permits copying and derivative works while the copyright notice and OASIS references are retained
records.finding: The useful part is the vocabulary rather than the XML. Splitting the enforcement point, which asks and then obeys, from the decision point, which answers, from the information point, which supplies the facts the answer needs, and from the administration point, which owns the rules, lets a venture say out loud where each of those four sits and notice when one of them is nowhere. The specification also insists that a decision has four outcomes rather than two, permit, deny, not-applicable and indeterminate, and that a combining algorithm has to say what happens when policies disagree or when evaluation fails, which is precisely the case an ad-hoc check leaves undefined.
records.applicability_limits: The wire format and policy language are heavy and largely out of fashion; nothing here argues for writing XACML. Thirteen years old with no revision, and the specification says nothing about multi-tenancy or about relationship-derived permissions.

records.source: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security (BCP 240)
records.licence: Copyright 2025 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors; subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust Legal Provisions
records.finding: A bearer token is a password with an expiry: whoever holds it is the user. The current practice therefore pushes towards binding a token to the client that was issued it, by mutual TLS or by proof of possession, so that a stolen token is not enough on its own. Two grants are ruled out rather than discouraged in practice: the password grant must not be used, because it hands the user's password to the client and cannot carry a second factor, and issuing tokens directly in an authorisation response should not be used. Refresh tokens held by a public client must be either bound to the client or rotated on each use.
records.applicability_limits: Normative for OAuth deployments and silent about everything else: it does not tell a venture whether to use OAuth at all, does not set token lifetimes, and does not address authorisation decisions beyond the scope of the token.

records.version_or_commit: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2, dated 15 December 2023
records.licence: OpenID Foundation copyright under the foundation's intellectual property policy. The notices appendix did not render at this access, so the exact reuse permission was not verified and no wording is carried here
records.finding: The two tokens answer different questions and confusing them is the classic integration bug. The identity token is a signed statement to one named client that a person authenticated, and the client is required to check that the audience claim carries its own client identifier; the access token is the thing a resource server accepts. A client that forwards its identity token to an API as if it were a credential has built an authentication system with no audience check at the point that matters. Where more attributes about the person are wanted, the user-information endpoint is what the access token is for.
records.applicability_limits: A protocol specification: it fixes token semantics and validation duties and says nothing about what the person is then allowed to do, which is the whole of the authorisation question.
records.review: on-change-of:a new OpenID Connect Core errata set or version

records.source: NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management
records.version_or_commit: Revision 4, final; the revision superseded the previous edition on 1 August 2025 and the HTML edition read here carries an August 2025 date
records.licence: United States Government work, not subject to domestic copyright
records.finding: Authentication strength is graded rather than binary, and the grade carries session consequences: the higher the assurance level, the shorter the maximum session life and the tighter the inactivity limit, running from a month at the lowest level to hours at the highest. Two positions are worth carrying into any venture. Phishing resistance is defined by binding the authenticator to the session, so anything a person can read and retype, one-time codes included, is not phishing-resistant however many digits it has. Authentication over the telephone network is a restricted authenticator rather than a forbidden one, and choosing it obliges the venture to offer something else as well.
records.applicability_limits: Written for United States federal agencies and their risk assessments; the assurance levels map onto federal impact categories, not onto a small venture's threat model, and adopting the numbers wholesale imports a process most ventures do not have.

records.source: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Session Management Cheat Sheet
records.version_or_commit: live page, no version or revision date shown on the document itself
records.finding: A server-side session is a small set of properties that are cheap to get right and expensive to retrofit: an identifier with real entropy from a cryptographic generator, a cookie marked secure and inaccessible to script and restricted in when the browser will send it cross-site, a fresh identifier issued whenever the privilege level changes, an idle limit and an absolute limit that both exist, and invalidation on the server at logout rather than deletion on the client. The guidance is direct that session credentials do not belong in browser storage reachable by script, which is the property that separates a cookie session from a token kept in local storage.
records.applicability_limits: Browser-centric. It has nothing to say about machine-to-machine calls, native clients that hold no cookie jar, or the cross-site cases a public API meets.

records.version_or_commit: PostgreSQL 18 current documentation, copyright 1996 to 2026 The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
records.finding: A row policy is a boolean expression the database applies before the query's own conditions, so the tenant predicate stops depending on any application author remembering it. The reason to read the documentation rather than the marketing is the list of things that walk straight past a policy: a superuser, any role carrying the bypass attribute, and by default the table's own owner, which is the role most applications connect as. Turning the owner's exemption off is a separate statement that has to be issued per table. Referential integrity checks also bypass policies by design, so a unique or foreign key constraint can confirm the existence of a row the querying tenant cannot see.
records.applicability_limits: PostgreSQL specific. Other engines offer the feature under other names with different bypass rules, and connection pooling that reuses one database role for every tenant defeats the whole mechanism unless the request's tenant is set per transaction.
records.counter_evidence: The documentation itself records a race in policies that read another table: a concurrent transaction can evaluate a policy against a snapshot in which a privilege has not yet been revoked, and the fixes offered cost locks or extra privileges. So the layer that makes isolation reliable has its own correctness conditions rather than being free.

records.source: Azure Architecture Center, Architectural approaches for storage and data in multitenant solutions
records.version_or_commit: article date 2025-07-17, page updated 2026-06-15, on a 365-day update cycle
records.licence: Microsoft copyright under the Microsoft Learn terms of use; no open reuse licence was read at this access
records.finding: The choice between one shared store, a shard holding several tenants, and a store per tenant is a trade of density against blast radius, and the deciding facts are dull ones: the hard scale ceiling of a single resource, whether tenants have their own keys, backup policies or data locations, and whether you can attribute consumption per tenant for billing. Two shapes are named as things to avoid outright, a table per tenant inside one database, and adding a column to satisfy one customer. The guidance is candid that row-level security requires the user's and the tenant's identity to be carried all the way from the request into every query, that this is hard to design, test and maintain, and that many multi-tenant systems therefore do not use it.
records.applicability_limits: Written against Azure services, so its concrete limits and pooling options are product-specific. The scale advice keys off tenant counts around fifty and above, which is the wrong end of the range for a venture with three customers.
records.counter_evidence: It undercuts the neatest recommendation in this area: pushing the tenant predicate into the database is the control most likely to hold, and the maintainer of one of the two databases that offer it reports that the propagation cost drives teams away from it. A control that is correct and unused is worth less than a weaker one that ships.

records.source: AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens, silo, pool and bridge models, with the 2020 tenant isolation whitepaper
records.version_or_commit: SaaS Lens, current revision at access. The companion whitepaper, SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies, is dated 1 August 2020 and is now labelled by AWS as for historical reference only
records.licence: Amazon Web Services documentation terms; no open reuse licence
records.finding: Three words settle most arguments about tenancy because they can be applied per component rather than per system: dedicated resources for a tenant, shared resources across tenants, and a deliberate mixture where a component's regulatory profile or noisy-neighbour behaviour decides which it gets. The point that stops the vocabulary being decoration is that dedicated resources still sit behind one shared onboarding, identity and operations path; the moment each customer gets its own version and its own operational life, the thing is a managed service and the economics of the model are gone.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor guidance framed around AWS services and around businesses large enough to have an onboarding pipeline. The detailed treatment is in a whitepaper its own publisher now marks as historical, so the depth behind the vocabulary is no longer maintained.
records.counter_evidence: The staleness is the finding as much as the content: the most cited public treatment of tenant isolation strategy is six years old and disclaimed by its publisher, which is a reason to treat the silo, pool and bridge vocabulary as a naming scheme rather than as current engineering advice.

records.source: Microsoft Entra ID documentation, Manage emergency access admin accounts
records.version_or_commit: article date 2026-06-04, page updated 2026-06-05; the article declares itself AI-assisted
records.licence: Microsoft copyright under the Microsoft Learn terms of use; no open reuse licence was read at this access
records.finding: Break-glass access is a designed path, not an exception someone improvises, and the design is a short checklist. At least two accounts so one lost credential is not a lockout. No dependency on the federated identity provider, because provider outage is one of the reasons the path exists. Credentials held by the organisation rather than by a person, and stored somewhere physical and separate. Authentication that differs from the one normal administrators use, so a single method failing does not take out both. Standing rather than on-request privilege, because the approval machinery may be exactly what is broken. Every sign-in alerts, every use gets a review afterwards that asks whether it was a drill, a real emergency or misuse, and the whole path is exercised at least every ninety days.
records.applicability_limits: Written for one vendor's directory and its conditional-access machinery, and for organisations with an administration team and a safe. A single-operator venture has to keep the shape and change the mechanism, and the article is declared AI-assisted, so it is vendor guidance rather than a standard.
records.counter_evidence: The guidance requires excluding these accounts from the policies that block or restrict sign-in, which means the highest-privilege accounts in the system are deliberately outside the control that protects every other account. It is honest that the compensation is a phishing-resistant credential plus alerting and review, so break-glass trades prevention for detection rather than being free.
